items.title: Personality Rights vs Freedom of Expression - Finding a balance
items.summary: John Stuart Mill The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it. Freedom of speech and expression has long been regarded as a cornerstone of constitutional democracy. In India, it is guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India, 1950, and embodies the liberty to communicate ideas, share information, and engage in creative expression. It has sought a direction to the Central government to frame, notify and operationalise a dedicated, comprehensive and enforceable regulatory framework to protect children on social media platforms. items.title: Can courts accept written statements beyond 120-day deadline? Delhi High Court larger bench to decide
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently referred to a larger bench the question of whether courts can permit defendants in civil suits to file their written statements beyond the prescribed 120-day deadline. [Yogesh Taneja v. Vinay Taneja] A Division Bench of Justices Vivek Chaudhary and Renu Bhatnagar expressed disagreement with earlier decisions of coordinate benches holding that the 120-day deadline under the Delhi High Court (Original Side) Rules, 2018 is mandatory and cannot be extended. The Court was of the prima facie view that the provision is procedural in nature and should be interpreted in accordance with Supreme Court judgments permitting extensions in exceptional circumstances. The Bench observed that the language of the Delhi High Court Rules was substantially similar to the corresponding provision of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), which the Supreme Court had interpreted as directory rather than mandatory. "Thus, applying the same principle, the only possible interpretation is that Rule 4 of DHC Rules is also directory in nature, leaving the same discretion with the High Court, as is available to any other Courts to which Order VIII Rule 1 CPC applies, " the Court said. Speaker ]. A Bench of Chief Justice SA Dharmadhikari and Justice Arul Murugan , however, also held that acceptance of the resignations did not render disqualification proceedings pending against the MLAs academic or infructuous. The Speaker must still adjudicate those proceedings, and his determination would carry the consequences prescribed under the Tenth Schedule (concerning political defection) of the Constitution, the Court said. The Court, therefore, directed the Speaker to decide the pending disqualification proceedings against the former AIADMK MLAs within two months.
